profile.freedomStatement: Being able to say yes to a trip without checking my bank balance first.

profileSummary.headline: Student building a first buffer and Japan fund

regions.summary: Get a clear picture of the $1,200 coming in and the $1,100 going out each month.
regions.why: You have about $100 left over each month, which is a savings rate of 8.3% — real, but thin enough that surprises can wipe it out. Seeing exactly where the $1,100 goes is the fastest way to protect that $100 and grow it. This is where your trip money will actually come from.

regions.summary: Build a 2-month emergency buffer of $2,200 so an unexpected bill doesn't derail the plan.
regions.why: You have $300 saved against a $2,200 target, so you're 13.6% of the way there and covered for about 0.27 months. You carry no debt, which is a big head start — the only gap is the $1,900 buffer. A buffer is what lets you say yes to a trip without panic later.

regions.summary: Turn the leftover $100 a month into an automatic habit that keeps building once the buffer is full.
regions.why: Your surplus is small, so the habit matters more than the amount right now. Once the $2,200 buffer is in place, the same $100 a month can be pointed at Japan and at learning how money grows over time. Consistency is the whole trick at your stage.

regions.summary: A $4,000 trip, currently $0 funded, roughly 40 months away at your present surplus.
regions.why: This goal is your freedom statement in real form — saying yes to a trip without checking your balance. At $100 a month the projection is about 40 months, so the lever isn't discipline, it's either more income or a smaller first version of the trip. Knowing that number now is far better than guessing.

regions.summary: Learn how investing works now, so it's familiar when you have money that isn't already spoken for.
regions.why: Your spare savings figure is $0 — every dollar you have is doing a job in the buffer or the Japan fund. That makes this a place to learn rather than act, and your moderate risk preference means the ideas will suit you when the time comes. Understanding compounding at 19 is worth a lot on its own.

regions.summary: Far off for now — property needs capital that is many multiples of your current position.
regions.why: A deposit typically runs into tens of thousands, and you currently have $300 saved with $100 a month spare. That's not a criticism, it's just arithmetic — this region is honestly low relevance today. It's here so you know what it would take if it ever becomes a goal.

regions.summary: The one branch that can meaningfully change your 40-month Japan timeline: extra income.
regions.why: With $1,200 in and $1,100 out, there isn't much left to squeeze from spending. Earning even a little more as a student changes the maths faster than anything else on this map. That's why this branch rates higher for you than the investing ones.

regions.summary: High volatility, and you have no spare savings — a topic to understand, not to act on.
regions.why: Your spare savings are $0 and your risk preference is moderate, so the size of the price swings here sits well outside what your situation can absorb. It's still worth understanding, because you'll hear about it constantly. Learning first costs you nothing.

regions.summary: The point where a trip is a decision, not a calculation.
regions.why: You described freedom as saying yes to a trip without checking your bank balance first. That arrives when the $2,200 buffer is behind you and the Japan fund is filled. Everything else on this map is just the road there.

bridges.requirement: Track a full month of spending and confirm your $100 monthly surplus.
bridges.relationship: Knowing your numbers is what makes a buffer target realistic
bridges.why: You can't build a $2,200 buffer on a surplus you haven't confirmed. Once you've watched a month of the $1,100 in real life, you'll know whether $100 is the true figure or an optimistic one. That honesty makes the next stage work.

bridges.relationship: A buffer is what stops a setback from eating your savings habit
bridges.why: Right now $1,900 stands between you and a full 2-month buffer. Until that gap closes, any surprise cost would come straight out of whatever else you're building. Closing it first protects everything after it.

bridges.requirement: Have an automatic monthly saving habit running.
bridges.relationship: The habit is the engine that fills the Japan fund
bridges.why: The Japan projection of 40 months assumes $100 arrives every single month without fail. A habit that runs on its own is what makes that projection real rather than hopeful. Set the engine, then point it at the trip.

bridges.requirement: Have an automatic monthly saving habit running.
bridges.relationship: Money that grows has to exist first
bridges.why: Your spare savings figure is $0, so there's nothing here to work with yet. Building the habit is what eventually creates money that isn't already committed. Until then, this branch is reading, not doing.

bridges.requirement: Have an automatic monthly saving habit running.
bridges.relationship: Property sits at the far end of the same saving habit
bridges.why: With $300 saved, property is a long way off, and that's completely normal at 19. The same monthly habit is the only path that ever leads here. Understanding it now costs nothing.

bridges.requirement: Have an automatic monthly saving habit running.
bridges.relationship: Extra income makes every other region move faster
bridges.why: Your surplus of $100 is the bottleneck in every projection on this map. Raising income is the branch with the biggest effect on your 40-month Japan timeline. It deserves your attention early.

bridges.requirement: Have an automatic monthly saving habit running.
bridges.relationship: Volatile assets sit beyond a settled buffer and habit
bridges.why: With $0 spare savings, this branch is purely educational for you today. The habit and the buffer come first because they're what absorbs a bad month. Learn the ideas while the stakes are zero.

bridges.requirement: Explore at least one realistic extra-income option.
bridges.relationship: Every extra dollar earned shortens the 40-month timeline
bridges.why: Japan needs $4,000 and you're at $0 funded. Extra income is the most direct lever you have on that number as a student. This bridge exists because the two are tied together.

bridges.relationship: The trip is the literal version of your freedom statement
bridges.why: You said freedom is saying yes to a trip without checking your balance first. Funding this goal is that sentence coming true. It's the last stretch of road into the city.

bridges.requirement: Complete the investing basics learning step.
bridges.relationship: Understanding compounding extends freedom beyond one trip
bridges.why: One trip is the first version of freedom; knowing how money grows is what makes later versions cheaper. At 19, time is the resource you have most of. Learning now is the highest-value thing on this branch.

steps.title: Watch one full month of spending
steps.description: Record every dollar of the roughly $1,100 you spend for one month, without changing anything yet.
steps.why: Your surplus of $100 is the difference between $1,200 in and $1,100 out — a thin margin where small leaks matter. Watching a month without judging it shows you which parts of the $1,100 are fixed and which are choices. You can't plan around numbers you haven't seen.

steps.title: Put a number on your freedom statement
steps.description: Write down what 'saying yes to a trip without checking my balance' would cost in dollars.
steps.why: You already know the Japan trip is $4,000, but freedom for you is broader than one trip. Naming the number turns a feeling into a target you can actually track. It also makes the 40-month projection feel like information rather than bad news.

steps.title: Confirm and ring-fence the $100
steps.description: Decide the amount you can reliably keep each month and separate it from your everyday spending money.
steps.why: A surplus that stays in your spending account tends to disappear into the $1,100. Keeping it apart is the simplest structural change available to you. It costs nothing and makes every later step possible.

steps.title: Build the $2,200 buffer
steps.description: Grow your savings from $300 towards the two-month target of $2,200.
steps.why: You're at 13.6% of your buffer and covered for about 0.27 months, which means one unexpected bill lands straight on your plans. Two months of expenses is the target because your income as a student can be irregular. Closing the $1,900 gap is the single biggest reduction in stress on this map.

steps.title: Choose a repeatable monthly amount
steps.description: Pick an amount you can move to savings every month even in a bad month, and start with that.
steps.why: Your capacity is tight, so an ambitious number you abandon is worse than a small number you keep. A figure that survives a quiet month is the one that actually closes the $1,900 gap. Momentum beats intensity here.

steps.title: Make the saving automatic
steps.description: Set the monthly transfer to happen on its own, right after income arrives.
steps.why: With only $100 of room, relying on willpower at the end of the month rarely works. Moving the money first means the rest of the budget adjusts around it. This one change is what makes every projection on this map credible.

steps.title: Review the gap between income and expenses
steps.description: Every few months, check whether the $100 gap has widened, narrowed or held steady.
steps.why: Your savings rate is 8.3%, and at 19 that number will move a lot as study and work change. Reviewing it keeps the plan matched to reality instead of to an old snapshot. It also shows you progress you might otherwise miss.

steps.title: Fund the $4,000 Japan trip
steps.description: Track the Japan fund from $0 towards the $4,000 target.
steps.why: The projection says about 40 months at your current surplus, and $0 is funded so far. Seeing the balance climb is what keeps a long goal alive. This is the goal you named first, so it gets its own tracker.

steps.title: Test a shorter version of the trip
steps.description: Work out what a shorter or cheaper first trip would cost and how many months that version takes.
steps.why: Forty months is a long wait when you're 19, and $4,000 is your estimate rather than a fixed price. A smaller first trip might arrive years sooner and still be the thing you wanted. Reviewing the target is as valid as chasing it.

steps.title: Learn how investing differs from saving
steps.description: Work through the basics of what investing is, what risk means, and how compounding builds over time.
steps.why: Your spare savings are $0, so this region is about understanding rather than committing anything. Learning the vocabulary now means that when money is free, the decisions feel familiar instead of intimidating. Time is the advantage you have at 19, and it's worth knowing why.

steps.title: See what a deposit actually requires
steps.description: Learn how home deposits are sized and what timeline they imply at different saving rates.
steps.why: With $300 saved and $100 a month spare, property is far away, and it's healthier to know that clearly than to wonder. Understanding the maths removes the pressure you might feel from other people's timelines. If it ever becomes a goal, you'll start informed.

steps.title: Find one way to add income
steps.description: Identify a realistic option that fits around study and could add to your $1,200 monthly income.
steps.why: Your expenses of $1,100 are mostly fixed, so cutting further has limited room. Adding income is the lever that moves the $2,200 buffer and the $4,000 trip at the same time. Even a modest increase reshapes the 40-month projection.

steps.title: Understand volatility before anything else
steps.description: Learn what drives the large price swings in digital assets and how that risk is usually described.
steps.why: You have $0 in spare savings and a moderate risk preference, so this sits outside what your situation can currently absorb. Understanding it protects you from decisions made on hype rather than information. There's no cost to learning while you have nothing at risk.

steps.title: Revisit your freedom statement
steps.description: Once the buffer and the trip are funded, rewrite what freedom means to you next.
steps.why: Your current statement is about saying yes to a trip without checking your balance. When that's true, the definition usually grows into something bigger. Rewriting it keeps the map yours rather than a leftover from age 19.

freedomCity.title: 🌴 Freedom City
freedomCity.narrative: Freedom City is the day "being able to say yes to a trip without checking my bank balance first" is simply true. It's built on a $2,200 buffer behind you and a $4,000 trip fully funded in front of you.

disclaimers: Free Me provides general financial education, not personal financial advice. It doesn't know your full circumstances — consider them, and seek licensed advice for decisions that matter to you.
